sections.text: यथा दीपो निवातस्थो नेङ्गते सोपमा स्मृता।
The wise man who has conquered his mind and is absorbed in the Self is as a lamp which does not flicker, since it stands sheltered from every wind.

There, where the whole nature is seen in the light of the Self, where the man abides within his Self and is satisfied there, its functions restrained by its union with the Divine, the mind finds rest.
When he enjoys the Bliss which passes sense, and which only the Pure Intellect can grasp, when he comes to rest within his own highest Self, never again will he stray from reality.

We had been discussing Chapter 6, Dhyana Yoga, Yoga of Meditation. And that happiness can only come if we become detached from our attachment to this world of objects and beings. But we still have to work in this world.
And therefore the simple definition given of a person who has achieved that detachment, whether you call him a yogi or a sannyasis, Anasritaha Karma, Falam Karyam Karautiya. One who acts in this world without depending on the fruits of actions, he is acting, but he is not dependent on what will come out of my actions. That anxiety is not there.
One who has achieved that state of mind control. He is a yogi or he is a sannyasi. Thats as simple a definition.
Then he says to achieve that state, obviously you have to go through several disciplines and practices. And all this is all about controlling your mind. Because all that we consider a happiness or unhappiness, sorrow or pleasure is all a mental state.
When that mental state is controlled, we can control whether we are in a happiness or unhappiness state. The practice given is called meditation. This meditation is not just a physical act of sitting down cross-legged and focusing on some idea, but regulating the entire life.
We have seen the prerequisites of what needs to be done. It is about one who regulates his life in all aspects. He does not eat too much, he does not eat too little, he does not sleep too much, he does not sleep too little.
Even in his activities, he does not exert himself too much. In other words, everything in moderation. All that really means is you apply the appropriate amount of effort -- not too much, not too little.
Its like tightening a bolt. If you tighten too much, its a problem. If you dont tighten enough, its a problem.
Only time it works perfectly is when it is appropriately tightened. So every activity of our life should be regulated to a point. But then your mind has to be focused or controlled and how do we control mind? And we have learned that the very nature of the mind, very definition of mind is mind is nothing but a flow of thoughts.
Mind is like a river. Water does not make a river, but a flowing water in one direction makes a river. So mind is nothing but the flow of thoughts -- in our case, flowing in many directions.
These thoughts are channelized into many channels, and each channel assumes that at its end there is happiness. If we channelize them to one particular point where happiness really lies -- which scripture says is within yourself -- that exercise of reverting your minds flow of thoughts from outward to inward is called meditation. To practice that, we have been given a prescription and detailed instruction.
Sit down erect so there is no discomfort in your body. There is no discomfort in the environment around you. And then focus your mind onto yourself.
That peace which you experience during that inward journey is yourself. And as the meditators of all ages have said, once you experience that peace, you will like to experience that over and over again. And then with that constant practice, you reach a point where that peace become permanent.
The last thing we have seen is: Yada viniyatam chittam atmani eva avatishthate -- when the mind rests in the self. Once the mind has found its final destination, where the peace lies, it does not want to go anywhere. If somebody says, Where do you want to buy a house in Richmond? -- once Ive decided the West End is the right place, Im not going to look around in Mechanicsville or Chesterfield, because I have already decided that the right place is the West End.
Once the mind decides that the real resting place where peace is, is in myself, it will not go anywhere else. Its just the very nature of the mind. So it says, once that mind rests in the self, free from longing -- Nihsprihah sarva kamebhyah -- all the desires up till now were for what? Everything I have done since I understood who I am, till last night or this morning, is to get happiness, to feel happy, to get peace in life.
And this peace is so elusive. The more you go after it, like a mirage, the more it runs away from you. Once you find a place where it is not a mirage, you will establish yourself in that.
Once you establish in that, there is no longing for any objects and desires. Then it is said he is united -- that is Yuktah. We are like lost children.
We are lost in this sansar, this mela, and we are seeking our own place, where our family is, where we came from. When we get united with that place, we find peace. A child will be lost in India festival and is crying profusely.
No matter what you tell him, give me chocolate. Nothing works till find my parent. And as soon as he finds his parents nothing can attract him but that peace.
When you find after that there is nothing else you will look for. So our nature is peace and therefore we are seeking peace. If our nature is not peace, we wouldnt be seeking peace.
My nature is health, therefore I am seeking health. So anything happens, I run to the doctor, run to whatever, fix me quickly, as quickly as you can. Everybody says antibiotics, read about antibiotics and all the perils of taking antibiotics.
The first thing I go and ask my doctor is give me the antibiotics as quickly and as powerful as possible. I want to get rid of whatever that is not health as quickly as possible. Because my real nature is health.
My real nature is not unhealthy. So I am always seeking what my true nature is. My true nature is peace.
And everything else in this world is giving me un peace. Once I unite with that peace, I am considered Yuktaha. This simile used is just as in a windless room the flame of a lamp does not flicker, it remains steady.
Yatra uparamate chittam nirdam yoga sevaya yatracha eva atmana tmanam pasyan atmani tushyade. So when the mind restrained by the practice of yoga attains quietude by when seeing the self by the self he satisfied by the self always seeking all our life is some satisfaction, some peace. We tried everywhere else but it was never complete.
It may come for a for a while as I said. As soon as I get that, the key of my first BMW in my hand, a complete peace in my mind. All that I want to achieve.
And the next moment the agitation starts again. As soon as he tells me what the insurance would be for this guy. But once I found that piece where? By the self satisfied by the self.
So yogi, once he practices this yoga to find his peace and he found it, he is now satisfied that the final state. These four verses basically describe what yoga is all about. We have this whole notion about yoga being sitting down in a lotus position.
But those are all practices to control your body, mind, and intellect. All agitations in my life come through my body, mind, and intellect. Either my body is not healthy, or my mind is not healthy.
Mind is okay, but ideas are not coming -- the intellect is struggling. Once those are controlled and peace comes, then I am a yogi. Sukham atyantikam yat tat buddhi grahyam atindriyam, vetti yatra na cha eva ayam sthitah chalati tattvatah.
This is like somebody who has gone to Hawaii and is explaining the joy. I had been to all these different destinations for vacation. He said, No, no, Rajan, forget about all of that. You just go to Hawaii one time and thats the end of the story. You wouldnt like to go anywhere else. So he explained and see, when you go there, they have all these things.
After that you never have to take a vacation anywhere else. Sukam Atyantikam Yattad When a yogi feels this infinite bliss, one who has experienced this bliss in his meditation, he said thats infinite bliss. That bliss is not something which comes and goes.
So what we worry about is: this is too much trouble in the first place. I cant wake up early in the morning as everybody says I should. Then I have to sit down in a particular place.
Then I have to control my mind, which is not controllable in the first place. And then someday Ill find a little peace and it will go away, and Ill have to start all over again. But the real meditation -- once a person has experienced that infinite bliss -- can be grasped by the intellect.
Buddhi grahyam atindriyam -- its not something promised that can never be proved. Used to say, In our business there is no danger because we can bluff our way out and nobody can catch us. But no, Bhagavan said thats not true. You will be able to grasp this peace through Buddhi, the intellect.
But that Buddhi is the pure Buddhi -- the intellect that is not clouded by Rajas and Tamas. We are also very smart at finding what is right and wrong for us. But all that right and wrong is colored by our vasanas.
What my Buddhi says is good for me or not good for me is all colored by my experiences, desires, and vasanas. The intellect which is pure will grasp that infinite happiness. Vetti yatra na cha eva ayam sthitah chalati tattvatah -- once Buddhi grasps that infinite peace, he will never be shaken from that ultimate reality.
Tattvatah -- he will never be able to think the other way around. He will never be able to think happiness lies outside. Because his Buddhi has grasped that the reality where the bliss is so thats a state which only you have to achieve one time.
Once you achieve that, nobody will be able to shake you off that realization. Once you realize what is reality. Once you wake up from your dream and you realize what the reality is.
No matter how much you convince yourself that no, no, no. The reality was the one which was experiencing the dream. In my dream I was Bill Gates boss.
No matter how much I convince myself that I am actually Bill Gates boss, thats not going to work. Because once my Buddhi has grasped that what I was experiencing was nothing but a dream, as a waker I will not be able to go back to that. In the same way, the Upanishad says that the waking world is a dream.
We have assigned values to all these objects in our waking world as if they are happiness. Once you wake up from this, you realize that there is no value outside for your own bliss or happiness. And from that you cannot be shaken off.
Yam labdhva cha aparam labham manyate na adhikam tatah -- having experienced that, you will realize there is nothing else greater to be achieved. All my life, everything I have done is to find some peace, some happiness. Well, here is ultimate happiness and ultimate bliss.
So there is nothing to be gained if I suddenly wake up and realize that my forefathers used to own the entire real estate in Richmond.

The beautiful simile in verse 19 - yatha dipo nivata-stho nengate - compares the controlled mind to a lamp in a windless place that does not flicker. Our minds currently flicker violently because the winds of desire constantly blow through them. One thought leads to another: Im chanting Rama, which reminds me of Ramlal who owes me money, which reminds me... The cascading associations carry us far from our intended focus. But when we calm the winds of desire, even briefly, the flame of awareness becomes steady.
Verse 21 promises sukham atyantikam - infinite, never-ending bliss. This is not exaggeration but precise description. The happiness we experience from external achievements - getting the car keys to our first BMW - is real but fleeting. The next moment, worries about insurance arise. The bliss discovered in meditation is different in kind, not just degree. It is buddhi-grahyam atindriyam - graspable by the pure intellect but beyond the senses. It cannot be seen, touched, or heard, yet it is more real than any sensory experience.
The promise of verse 21 is crucial: Sthitash chalati tattvatah - once established in this truth, the yogi never strays from reality. This is like waking from a dream. No matter how vivid the dream was - even if you were Bill Gates boss in it - once awake, you cannot convince yourself the dream was real. The waking state has superior claim to reality. Similarly, the one who has tasted this infinite bliss through meditation can never again believe that happiness lies in external objects. Today, sit quietly and ask: What would it mean to find a happiness that never ends? Let that question draw you inward.
